title: Shapes & Symmetry
blurb: Naming 2-D shapes by their sides, right angles as quarter turns, sorting quadrilaterals, the fold test for line symmetry, and the faces, edges and vertices of 3-D solids.

lessons.title: 2-D Shapes
lessons.concreteComparison: Lay three straight sticks on the ground so they close up into a ring: a triangle. Add a fourth stick: a quadrilateral. Five sticks: a pentagon. Six: a hexagon. A shape's name is nothing more than a COUNT of its straight sides — and wherever two sticks meet, a corner appears, so the corners always match the sides, one for one.
lessons.objective: Name 2-D shapes by counting their straight sides — triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon — and check that every shape has exactly as many corners (vertices) as sides.
concept: **The name is a count.** Three straight sides make a triangle, four a quadrilateral, five a pentagon, six a hexagon. Nothing else about the shape — big or small, tall or squashed, tilted or upright — changes its name.

**Sides come with corners.** Walk around the boundary: every side ends exactly where the next one starts, at a corner (a VERTEX). So a pentagon has $5$ corners, a hexagon $6$ — the two counts can never differ.
**Only straight sides count.** A circle has no straight sides at all, so it earns no side-count name — it is not a polygon. And a shape must CLOSE: sticks that leave a gap make no shape yet.
lessons.keyIdea: Count the straight sides: three is a triangle, four a quadrilateral, five a pentagon, six a hexagon — and the corners always match the count, side for side.

facts.title: Names by side count
facts.explanation: The name is the count — nothing more, nothing less.

facts.title: Sides = corners
facts.explanation: Each side ends at the corner where the next one starts, so the counts match.

workedExamples.statement: A shape has $5$ straight sides. Name it, and count its corners without looking at it.
workedExamples.note: Every side has two ends; every corner joins exactly two ends.
workedExamples.solution: Five sides: a PENTAGON. Its $5$ sides have $5 \times 2 = 10$ ends, and every corner is a meeting of exactly $2$ ends: $10 \div 2 = 5$ corners. Sides and corners always match.

workedExamples.statement: A triangle and a hexagon are drawn side by side. How many sides in total — and how many corners in total?
workedExamples.solution: Sides: $3 + 6 = 9$. Corners match sides shape by shape ($3$ and $6$), so the corner total is the same $9$.

commonMistakes.text: Calling every four-sided shape a square.
commonMistakes.correction: Quadrilateral is the family name for ANY four straight sides. A square is one strict member of that family — most quadrilaterals are not squares.

commonMistakes.text: Thinking a triangle standing on its point is a different shape.
commonMistakes.correction: The name counts sides, not which way is up. Turn a triangle any way you like — three sides, three corners, still a triangle.

tryIt.statement: A hexagon and a quadrilateral stand together. How many sides do they have between them?
tryIt.solution: $6 + 4 = 10$ sides (and $10$ corners too, since each shape's corners match its sides).

tryIt.statement: A shape has $6$ corners. Name it and count its sides.
tryIt.solution: Six corners means six sides: a HEXAGON. Receipt: $6$ sides have $6 \times 2 = 12$ ends, and $12 \div 2 = 6$ corners — the counts agree.

steps.title: Count the straight sides
beats: A shape keeps its promises — and the first promise is its NAME: count the straight sides. Three sides: triangle. Four: quadrilateral. Five: pentagon. Six: hexagon.
Nothing else matters for the name — not the size, not the colour, not which way up it sits. A squashed triangle and a tall one are both triangles.
Only STRAIGHT sides count, and the shape must close into a ring. A circle has no straight sides, so it takes no side-count name.

steps.title: Naming shapes
steps.intro: Count the sides; the count is the name.

examples.prompt: Name the shape in the picture, and count its corners.
steps: Five straight sides: a pentagon.
Corners match sides: $5 \times 2 = 10$ side-ends, $10 \div 2 = 5$ corners.

examples.prompt: A triangle road sign and a hexagon tile: how many sides in total?
steps: Count each: $3$ and $6$.
Together: $3 + 6 = 9$ sides — and $9$ corners too.

steps.title: Count and name
steps.intro: Sides first, name second.

problems.prompt: The shape in the picture has $4$ straight sides. It is a:
problems.explanation: Four straight sides: a quadrilateral — the family name for every four-sided shape. Receipt: $4 \times 2 = 8$ side-ends, $8 \div 2 = 4$ corners.

problems.prompt: A pentagon has how many more sides than a triangle?
problems.explanation: $5 - 3 = 2$ more sides. Check by adding back: $2 + 3 = 5$ ✓.

problems.prompt: Which shape has the MOST corners?
problems.explanation: Corners match sides, so compare side counts: $6 > 5 > 4$ — the hexagon wins.

steps.title: Corners without counting
steps.prompt: A polygon has $8$ straight sides. How many vertices must it have?
steps.explanation: Sides and vertices always match: $8$ sides have $8 \times 2 = 16$ ends, and each vertex joins exactly $2$ ends — $16 \div 2 = 8$ vertices. ($16$ counts the side-ENDS, not the corners.)

steps.title: The names tell on themselves
steps.body: POLYGON is Greek for "many angles" — and the shape names carry their counts openly: TRIangle is three angles, PENTAgon five, HEXAgon six. QUADRILATERAL switches to Latin and counts sides instead: four of them. Say the name slowly and it counts itself for you.

steps.title: Corners match sides — the receipt
beats: Here is why the counts can never differ. Every side has $2$ ends. A hexagon's $6$ sides have $6 \times 2 = 12$ ends.
Every corner is a meeting place of exactly $2$ ends — one side arriving, the next one leaving. So the corners number $12 \div 2 = 6$: the same as the sides.
This works for every polygon: double the sides, halve the ends, and you have counted the corners without touching the picture.

steps.title: The side-ends receipt
steps.intro: Double the sides, halve the result — that counts the corners.

examples.prompt: Count the sides and vertices of the hexagon in the picture.
steps: Six straight sides. Ends: $6 \times 2 = 12$.
Vertices: $12 \div 2 = 6$ — sides and corners match.

examples.prompt: A polygon has $9$ sides. How many corners?
steps: Ends: $9 \times 2 = 18$.
Corners: $18 \div 2 = 9$ — always the same as the sides.

steps.title: Receipt the corners
steps.intro: Sides and vertices — one count, two names.

problems.prompt: A hexagon has how many vertices?
problems.explanation: Same as its sides: $6$. The $12$ counts side-ends ($6 \times 2$) — halve it to land on the corners.

problems.prompt: Two pentagons stand side by side. Total vertices:
problems.explanation: Each pentagon carries $5$ vertices: $2 \times 5 = 10$.

problems.prompt: For the triangle in the picture, sides plus vertices makes:
problems.explanation: Three sides and three matching vertices: $3 + 3 = 6$.

steps.title: One count, two names
steps.prompt: A quadrilateral's sides and vertices together number:
steps.explanation: Four sides, four matching vertices: $4 + 4 = 8$. (Answering $4$ counts only one of the two; $16$ doubles everything.)

steps.title: What you learned
points: The name is a count: 3 triangle, 4 quadrilateral, 5 pentagon, 6 hexagon.
Size, colour and which-way-up never change the name.
Corners (vertices) always match sides — every side ends where the next begins.
The receipt: sides times 2 ends, divided by 2, counts the corners.
Only straight sides count, and the shape must close — a circle is not a polygon.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every shape below, touch each side as you count it — then say the name. Count first, name second, every time.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Names, counts, and the receipt together.

problems.prompt: A hexagon has how many more sides than a pentagon?
The picture shows a shape with $4$ straight sides. Its name is:
problems.explanation: Four sides — a quadrilateral, whatever its slant. Receipt: $4 \times 2 = 8$ ends, $8 \div 2 = 4$ corners.

problems.prompt: One triangle, one quadrilateral, one pentagon and one hexagon: total sides?
problems.explanation: $3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 18$ sides — and $18$ corners across the four shapes too.

problems.prompt: Which of these is NOT a polygon?
problems.explanation: A polygon needs at least $3$ straight sides; a circle has $0$ straight sides — no straight sides, no side-count name.

problems.prompt: A polygon has $10$ sides. Its vertices number:
problems.explanation: The receipt: $10 \times 2 = 20$ side-ends, $20 \div 2 = 10$ vertices — corners match sides, always.

steps.title: You've finished "2-D Shapes"
steps.body: Count the sides and the shape names itself — the first promise a shape keeps. Next: the corner every builder trusts — the right angle, a quarter of a full turn.

lessons.title: Right Angles
lessons.concreteComparison: Stand facing the ger door, then turn until you face the wall beside it: a QUARTER of a full spin. That turn has a name — the RIGHT angle — and you carry a tester everywhere: the corner of this page. Slide the page corner into any corner of the room; if it fits exactly, the corner is right. Four quarter turns bring you back to the door: four right angles fill a full turn.
lessons.objective: Recognise a right angle as a quarter turn, test corners with the page corner, and sort angles as smaller than, equal to, or bigger than a right angle.
concept: **A right angle is a quarter turn.** A full spin measures $360$ degrees, and a quarter of it is $90$: $4 \times 90 = 360$. The page's corner, the window's corner, the cross on squared paper — all right angles.

**The page corner is your tester.** Slide it into a corner: fits exactly — right angle; a gap is left over — the angle is SMALLER than right; the page corner sinks in with room to spare — BIGGER than right.
**Two right angles make a straight line.** Half a spin: $2 \times 90 = 180$. So a straight line holds two page corners, and a full turn holds four.
lessons.keyIdea: A right angle is a quarter of a full turn — 90 degrees; two of them make a straight line (180) and four fill the whole turn (360). Test the corners with the page corner.

facts.title: The quarter turn
facts.explanation: Four page corners around one point fill a complete spin.

facts.title: The straight line
facts.explanation: Two right angles side by side flatten into a straight line — half a turn.

workedExamples.statement: Four streets meet at a crossing, and every corner passes the page-corner test. Show that the four corners together make one full turn.
workedExamples.note: A right angle is a quarter turn; count the quarters.
workedExamples.solution: Each corner is a right angle: $90$ degrees, a quarter turn. Four quarters: $4 \times 90 = 360$ degrees — one complete spin, exactly. And $360 \div 4 = 90$ confirms each corner's share.

workedExamples.statement: Two right angles sit side by side. What do they make together?
workedExamples.solution: $90 + 90 = 180$ degrees — half a full turn, which is a STRAIGHT line. That is why a straight edge holds exactly two page corners: $180 \div 90 = 2$.

commonMistakes.text: Thinking a right angle tilted on its side stops being right.
commonMistakes.correction: A quarter turn is a quarter turn whichever way the arms point. Test with the page corner, not with "does it look like an upright L".

commonMistakes.text: Judging an angle by the length of its arms — long arms, big angle.
commonMistakes.correction: An angle is the TURN between the arms, not their length. The page-corner test ignores arm length completely — that is why it works.

tryIt.statement: How many right angles fit along a straight line? And in a full turn?
tryIt.solution: A straight line is half a turn: $2 \times 90 = 180$, so $2$ right angles. A full turn: $4 \times 90 = 360$, so $4$.

tryIt.statement: An angle is bigger than the page corner but smaller than a straight line. How much room lies between those two landmarks?
tryIt.solution: Between the quarter turn ($90$) and the half turn ($180$) lies $180 - 90 = 90$ degrees — a whole extra quarter turn of room. Check: $90 + 90 = 180$ ✓.

steps.title: The quarter turn and its tester
beats: Test the corners — that is this lesson's promise. A full spin is $360$ degrees; a QUARTER of it is the RIGHT angle: $90$ degrees, because $4 \times 90 = 360$.
Your tester travels with you: the page's corner. Fits a corner exactly — right angle. Gap left over — smaller than right. Sinks in with room to spare — bigger than right.
The arms' length never votes: an angle is TURN, not ink. A tiny drawn corner can hold a bigger turn than a huge one.

steps.title: Testing corners
steps.intro: Fit the page corner; read the result.

examples.prompt: The angle at $O$ in the picture fits the page corner exactly. Name it — and say how many like it fill a full turn.
steps: An exact fit: a RIGHT angle, $90$ degrees.
A full turn is $360$: $360 \div 90 = 4$ of them fill it, since $4 \times 90 = 360$.
examples.answer: a right angle; $4$ fill a full turn

examples.prompt: The hands of a clock at 3:00 — what angle do they make?
steps: The minute hand points straight up, the hour hand a quarter of the way round.
A quarter of the full face: $360 \div 4 = 90$ degrees — a right angle.

steps.title: Quarter-turn thinking
steps.intro: Fit the tester, count the quarters.

problems.prompt: Four right angles together make:
problems.explanation: Four quarters make one whole spin: $4 \times 90 = 360$ degrees.

problems.prompt: You slide the page corner into the angle at $O$ in the picture, and a gap is left over. The angle is:
problems.explanation: A leftover gap means the angle did not use the whole quarter turn — it is smaller than right. (This one is half a right angle: $90 \div 2 = 45$, and $45 < 90$.)

problems.prompt: Two right angles side by side make:
problems.explanation: $90 + 90 = 180$ degrees — half a turn, flat as a stretched rope.

steps.title: The page-corner test
steps.prompt: You slide the page's corner into a door-frame corner and it fits exactly. The door frame's corner is:
options: a right angle — a quarter turn
steps.explanation: An exact fit IS the definition: the corner holds exactly one quarter of a spin, $360 \div 4 = 90$ degrees. Door frames are built that way on purpose — doors only swing cleanly in right-angled frames.

steps.title: Why "RIGHT"?
steps.body: The name comes from Latin RECTUS — upright. A post standing properly on flat ground makes this angle with it, so it became the "upright" angle. Builders still check it constantly: a wall that misses the right angle by even a little leans, and a leaning wall is a falling wall on a slow schedule.

steps.title: Smaller, bigger, and the two landmarks
beats: Every angle can be sorted against the quarter turn: smaller than $90$, exactly $90$, or bigger. The page corner sorts them without measuring.
The landmarks stack: two right angles make a straight line ($2 \times 90 = 180$), and four fill the full turn ($4 \times 90 = 360$). The picture shows all four quarters around one point.
So an angle bigger than right but smaller than straight lives between the landmarks — the room between them is exactly one more quarter: $180 - 90 = 90$.

steps.title: Between the landmarks
steps.intro: Quarter, half, whole — sort every angle against them.

examples.prompt: A gate swings from closed through a quarter turn, then onward to a half turn. How much more did it turn after the quarter?
steps: From $90$ to $180$: the extra is $180 - 90 = 90$ degrees.
Another whole quarter turn — check: $90 + 90 = 180$ ✓.
examples.answer: $90$ degrees more — one more quarter turn

examples.prompt: At 6:00 the clock's hands point opposite ways — a straight angle. How many right angles is that?
steps: A straight angle is $180$ degrees.
$180 \div 90 = 2$ — two page corners, laid flat together.

steps.title: Sort against the landmarks
steps.intro: Smaller than 90, exactly 90, or between 90 and 180?

problems.prompt: A straight line holds how many right angles?
problems.explanation: $180 \div 90 = 2$. (Four is the FULL turn's count.)

problems.prompt: The page corner sinks fully into the angle at $O$ in the picture, with room to spare — yet the angle is not flat. The angle is:
options: bigger than a right angle, smaller than a straight one
problems.explanation: Room to spare means more than the quarter turn; not yet flat means less than the half. It lives between the landmarks — and the room between them is one more quarter: $180 - 90 = 90$.

problems.prompt: Three quarters of a full turn are used up. What remains?
problems.explanation: $360 - 3 \times 90 = 360 - 270 = 90$ — exactly one more quarter. Check: $270 + 90 = 360$ ✓.

steps.title: Quarter by quarter
steps.prompt: A dancer makes a quarter turn four times, always the same way. She now faces:
options: the way she started — a full turn
a quarter turn from the start
steps.explanation: Four quarters make one whole: $4 \times 90 = 360$ degrees, a complete spin back to the start. (Two quarters would face her the opposite way: $2 \times 90 = 180$.)

steps.title: What you learned
points: A right angle is a quarter of a full turn: 90 degrees, since 4 × 90 = 360.
The page corner tests any corner: exact fit, gap (smaller), or room to spare (bigger).
Two right angles make a straight line: 2 × 90 = 180.
Arm length never votes — an angle is turn, not ink.
Tilting a right angle does not un-right it; the tester works at any slant.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every angle below, say the tester's verdict first — fits, gap, or room to spare — then pick the answer. The verdict IS the answer.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Quarters, halves, and the tester's verdicts.

problems.prompt: The hands of a clock make a right angle at:
problems.explanation: At 3:00 the hands are a quarter of the face apart: $360 \div 4 = 90$ degrees. (6:00 makes a straight angle; at 12:00 the hands lie together.)

problems.prompt: Two right angles plus one more right angle make:
problems.explanation: $3 \times 90 = 270$ degrees — three quarters. One more quarter would close the spin: $270 + 90 = 360$.

problems.prompt: Every corner of the window in the picture passes the page-corner test. All four corners together make:
problems.explanation: Four right angles: $4 \times 90 = 360$ degrees — one full turn shared out among the window's corners.

problems.prompt: An angle smaller than a right angle is ALWAYS smaller than a straight angle too, because:
options: the quarter turn is smaller than the half turn
all angles are smaller than straight ones
problems.explanation: Under $90$ means under $180$ as well — the landmarks sit in order, quarter before half: $90 < 180$, and the gap between them is $180 - 90 = 90$.

problems.prompt: How many quarter turns fit in TWO full turns?
problems.explanation: Two spins: $2 \times 360 = 720$ degrees; $720 \div 90 = 8$ quarters.

steps.title: You've finished "Right Angles"
steps.body: The quarter turn, the tester in every book's corner, and the landmarks at 90, 180 and 360. Next: the shapes those corners build — the quadrilateral family, sorted by its rules.

lessons.title: Sorting Quadrilaterals
lessons.concreteComparison: Four-sided shapes are one big family. The square window, the long rectangular door, the leaning fence panel — all quadrilaterals. The square is the STRICTEST member: four equal sides AND four right angles. The rectangle keeps the right angles but lets opposite sides pair up long-and-short. The leaning panel keeps only the count of four. Stricter rules make a smaller club — and since the square obeys every rectangle rule, every square IS a rectangle.
lessons.objective: Sort quadrilaterals by their rules — four equal sides and four right angles for a square, right angles with opposite sides equal for a rectangle — and explain why every square is also a rectangle.
concept: **Quadrilateral is the family name.** Any closed shape with $4$ straight sides belongs — leaning, stretched, or neat. Four sides, four corners, no other requirement.

**A rectangle passes two tests.** All four corners pass the page-corner test ($4 \times 90 = 360$, a full turn of right angles), and opposite sides are equal — the top matches the bottom, the left matches the right.

**A square is a rectangle with a bonus.** It passes both rectangle tests AND makes all four sides equal. Stricter rules, smaller club: every square is a rectangle, but most rectangles are not squares.
lessons.keyIdea: Sort by rules, not by looks: four straight sides makes a quadrilateral, right angles with opposite sides equal makes a rectangle, and equal sides on top of that makes a square — so every square is a rectangle.

facts.title: The rectangle's two tests
facts.explanation: Four page-corner angles, and sides matching in opposite pairs.

facts.title: The square's bonus
facts.explanation: Every square passes every rectangle test — membership nests one way.

workedExamples.statement: A square is drawn with corners at $(2, 2)$, $(8, 2)$, $(8, 8)$ and $(2, 8)$. Show that its bottom side and its left side really are equal.
workedExamples.note: Read each side's length off the coordinates.
workedExamples.solution: Bottom: from $2$ across to $8$ is $8 - 2 = 6$. Left: from $2$ up to $8$ is the same $8 - 2 = 6$. Equal — and the add-back check $6 + 2 = 8$ signs the receipt. With all four corners right, the shape earns its name.

workedExamples.statement: A rectangle is drawn with corners at $(1, 1)$, $(9, 1)$, $(9, 5)$ and $(1, 5)$. Show its opposite sides are equal — and say why it is NOT a square.
workedExamples.note: Compare bottom with top, then long side with short.
workedExamples.solution: Bottom and top both run from $1$ to $9$: $9 - 1 = 8$ each (add back: $8 + 1 = 9$ ✓). Left and right both run from $1$ to $5$: $5 - 1 = 4$ each ($4 + 1 = 5$ ✓). Opposite sides equal, four right angles: a rectangle. But $8 > 4$ — neighbouring sides differ, so it is not a square.

commonMistakes.text: Saying a square is not a rectangle.
commonMistakes.correction: The rectangle test asks only for right angles and opposite sides equal. A square passes both — its equal sides are a bonus, not a disqualification. Every square is a rectangle.

commonMistakes.text: Calling a square standing on its corner a "diamond" — a different shape.
commonMistakes.correction: Turning a shape changes nothing it promised: the sides stay equal, the corners stay right. A tilted square is a square.

tryIt.statement: A quadrilateral has four right angles and sides $7$, $3$, $7$, $3$. Which family member is it — and why not a square?
tryIt.solution: Right angles ($4 \times 90 = 360$) and opposite sides equal: a RECTANGLE. Not a square, because neighbouring sides differ: $7 > 3$.

tryIt.statement: True or false: every square is a rectangle.
tryIt.solution: True. The rectangle test has $2$ parts — right angles, opposite sides equal — and a square passes $1 + 1 = 2$ of them, both. The bonus (ALL sides equal) breaks no rule.

steps.title: The family and the rectangle's rules
beats: Count the sides, test the corners — both promises work together here. Any $4$ straight sides make a QUADRILATERAL: the family name. The picture's leaning shape belongs, with no equal sides and no right angles at all.

The RECTANGLE is the family's tidy member. Two tests: every corner passes the page-corner test ($4 \times 90 = 360$ — a full turn of right angles), and opposite sides are equal, top matching bottom, left matching right.
Sort by RULES, never by looks. A long thin rectangle and a nearly-square one pass exactly the same two tests.

steps.title: Running the tests
steps.intro: Right angles first, then match the opposite sides.

examples.prompt: The rectangle in the picture has corners $(1, 1)$, $(9, 1)$, $(9, 5)$, $(1, 5)$. Check its opposite sides.
steps: Bottom and top: $9 - 1 = 8$ each (add back $8 + 1 = 9$ ✓).
Left and right: $5 - 1 = 4$ each ($4 + 1 = 5$ ✓). Opposite pairs match — rectangle confirmed.
examples.answer: opposite sides $8$ and $8$, $4$ and $4$ — a rectangle

examples.prompt: A fence panel has four equal sides of $5$, but its corners fail the page-corner test. Is it a square?
steps: The square test has two parts: equal sides AND right angles — $1 + 1 = 2$ tests.
This panel passes only the sides test: $1$ of $2$. Not a square — just a leaning equal-sided quadrilateral.
examples.answer: no — equal sides alone pass only $1$ of the $2$ tests

steps.title: Which member?
steps.intro: Rules decide, looks distract.

problems.prompt: The shape in the picture has four right angles, long sides $8$ and short sides $4$. It is a:
problems.explanation: Right angles ($4 \times 90 = 360$) and opposite sides equal: rectangle. Not a square — $8 > 4$, the neighbouring sides differ.

problems.prompt: Which rule does EVERY quadrilateral obey?
problems.explanation: The family asks only for the count: $4$ sides (and the matching $4$ corners — $4 \times 2 = 8$ side-ends, $8 \div 2 = 4$). Right angles and equal sides are extra rules for stricter members.

problems.prompt: A rectangle's bottom side is $9$ cm. Its top side is:
problems.explanation: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so the top copies the bottom exactly: $9$ cm. The two differ by nothing at all — $9 - 9 = 0$, and adding back, $0 + 9 = 9$ ✓.

steps.title: Rules, not looks
steps.prompt: A quadrilateral has four page-corner angles, opposite sides equal, long side $7$, short side $4$. It is:
steps.explanation: Both rectangle tests pass: rectangle. The square would demand equal neighbours, but $7 > 4$. And with four sides it is certainly no pentagon — $4 < 5$.

steps.title: The chessboard's square of squares
steps.body: A chessboard is a square cut into $8$ rows of $8$ squares: $8 \times 8 = 64$ little squares sitting inside one big one. Squares tile perfectly — right angles meeting right angles, $4 \times 90 = 360$ around every inner corner, no gaps anywhere. That is why floors, windows and game boards love them.

steps.title: The square — strictest of the family
beats: The SQUARE passes the rectangle's two tests and adds a bonus: ALL four sides equal. In the picture the bottom is $8 - 2 = 6$ and the left is the same $8 - 2 = 6$ — drawn honestly square.
Because it passes every rectangle test, every square IS a rectangle. The reverse fails: a rectangle with sides $8$ and $4$ is no square, since $8 > 4$.
And tilting changes nothing: stand a square on its corner and its sides are still equal, its corners still right. Rules travel with the shape.

steps.title: Membership runs one way
steps.intro: Squares pass rectangle tests; rectangles may fail the square's.

examples.prompt: A student says: "a square is not a rectangle." Test the square against the rectangle's rules.
steps: Right angles? Yes — all four, $360 \div 90 = 4$ of them.
Opposite sides equal? Yes — ALL its sides are equal, so opposite pairs certainly match. Both tests passed: $1 + 1 = 2$. The student is wrong.
examples.answer: the square passes both tests — it IS a rectangle

examples.prompt: A rectangle has sides $8$, $4$, $8$, $4$. Does it pass the square's test?
steps: The square demands all sides equal — but $8 > 4$.
It stays a rectangle. Membership runs one way only: squares into rectangles, not back.
examples.answer: no — $8 > 4$, so it is a rectangle but not a square

steps.title: The strictest member
steps.intro: Two tests plus a bonus.

problems.prompt: Every square is a rectangle because:
problems.explanation: Right angles — check. Opposite sides equal — check (all of them are). $1 + 1 = 2$ tests passed; the bonus breaks nothing.

problems.prompt: The shape in the picture stands on its corner: four equal sides, four page-corner angles. It is:
problems.explanation: Equal sides AND right angles: a square, whichever way it stands. Turning a shape cancels none of its promises — $4 \times 90 = 360$ still.

problems.prompt: A quadrilateral has four equal sides but NO right angles. Is it a square?
options: no — a square needs right angles too
yes, if it is drawn neatly
problems.explanation: The square test has $2$ parts; equal sides pass only $1$ of them, and $2 - 1 = 1$ test still fails. No right angles, no square.

steps.title: One-way membership
steps.prompt: Every square is a rectangle. Is every rectangle a square?
options: no — its neighbouring sides may differ
no rectangle is ever a square
steps.explanation: A rectangle with sides $8$ and $4$ passes both rectangle tests yet fails the square's bonus: $8 > 4$. Membership nests one way — the strictest member fits inside every looser club, never the reverse.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Quadrilateral is the family name: any 4 straight sides.
Rectangle: four right angles (4 × 90 = 360) and opposite sides equal.
Square: a rectangle whose sides are ALL equal — the strictest member.
Every square is a rectangle; a rectangle with unequal neighbours is not a square.
Sort by rules, never by looks — and tilting changes nothing.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each shape below, run the tests out loud in order: sides straight and four? corners right? opposite sides equal? all sides equal? Stop at the strictest test it passes.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: The whole family, sorted by rules.

problems.prompt: Which shape does NOT belong to the quadrilateral family?
problems.explanation: The family badge is four sides — a triangle carries only $3$, and $3 < 4$. Rectangles and squares are members in good standing.

problems.prompt: The rectangle in the picture has corners $(2, 3)$, $(9, 3)$, $(9, 7)$, $(2, 7)$. Its top side measures:
problems.explanation: The top runs from $2$ to $9$: $9 - 2 = 7$ (add back: $7 + 2 = 9$ ✓) — equal to the bottom, as a rectangle promises. The short sides measure $7 - 3 = 4$ each ($4 + 3 = 7$ ✓).

problems.prompt: A square has sides of $6$; a rectangle has sides $8$ and $4$. Which statement is right?
options: both are rectangles; only the first is a square
problems.explanation: The square passes both rectangle tests ($1 + 1 = 2$) plus its bonus. The $8$-by-$4$ shape is a rectangle only: $8 > 4$.

problems.prompt: The four right angles of a rectangle together make:
problems.explanation: $4 \times 90 = 360$ degrees — the same full turn the crossing's corners made in the last lesson.

problems.prompt: The leaning shape in the picture has $4$ straight sides, no equal sides, no right angles. Its best name is:
problems.explanation: It passes only the family test: four sides (receipt: $4 \times 2 = 8$ side-ends, $8 \div 2 = 4$ corners). No stricter club will take it.

steps.title: You've finished "Sorting Quadrilaterals"
steps.body: Rules, not looks — and the strictest member fits inside every looser club. Next promise to test: the fold. Some shapes hide a mirror down their middle.

lessons.title: Line Symmetry
lessons.concreteComparison: Cut a shape out of paper and fold it down the middle. If the two halves lie EXACTLY on top of each other — every edge on an edge, no overhang anywhere — the fold line is a LINE OF SYMMETRY: the shape's hidden mirror. Butterfly wings match this way, and so do the felt patterns sewn on a ger door. The fold test never lies: exact match, or no mirror.
lessons.objective: Use the fold test to find lines of symmetry, draw mirror lines through the true middle of a shape, and count the lines a shape has — 0 for a scalene triangle, 1 for an isosceles triangle, 2 for a rectangle, 4 for a square.
concept: **The fold test.** Fold the shape along a line: halves match exactly — the line is a line of symmetry; any overhang at all — it is not. Try the fold, and the shape answers.

**The mirror line is exact.** It must pass through the TRUE middle. For a shape sitting from $2$ across to $8$, the vertical mirror stands at the halfway mark: $2 + 8 = 10$, and $10 \div 2 = 5$. A line drawn roughly nearby fails the fold.

**Shapes carry counts.** A scalene triangle: $0$ lines. An isosceles triangle: $1$. A rectangle: $2$ (NOT its diagonals). A square: the rectangle's $2$ plus $2$ diagonals $= 4$. The count is a property you can check fold by fold.
lessons.keyIdea: Try the fold: halves matching exactly make a line of symmetry, the line passes the true middle, and counting the folds that work gives each shape its symmetry number: scalene triangle 0, isosceles 1, rectangle 2, square 4.

facts.title: The fold test
facts.explanation: Each matching half is one half of the whole — and two exact halves rebuild it.

facts.title: Symmetry counts
facts.explanation: The square keeps the rectangle's two lines and adds its two diagonals.

workedExamples.statement: A rectangle (longer than it is wide) — how many lines of symmetry, and why are its diagonals NOT among them?
workedExamples.note: Try all the folds; keep only exact matches.
workedExamples.solution: Two folds work: side-middle to side-middle, across and down. The diagonal fold makes the two triangle halves stick out past each other — overhang, so it fails. Count: $2$. (A square would add its $2$ diagonals: $2 + 2 = 4$.)

workedExamples.statement: Count the lines of symmetry of the block letters A, H and F — and give the total.
workedExamples.note: Fold each letter in your head; count exact matches only.
workedExamples.solution: A: one vertical mirror — $1$. H: vertical AND horizontal — $2$. F: no fold matches — $0$. Total: $1 + 2 + 0 = 3$.

commonMistakes.text: Folding a rectangle along its diagonal and calling it a line of symmetry.
commonMistakes.correction: Fold it with real paper once: the halves overhang. A rectangle has exactly 2 lines, both through the middles of its sides. Only the SQUARE earns diagonal mirrors.

commonMistakes.text: Drawing the mirror line roughly near the middle.
commonMistakes.correction: The fold test is exact: the line must pass the true middle (halfway between 2 and 8 is exactly 5, not "about there"). A line slightly off fails the fold.

tryIt.statement: How many lines of symmetry has a square?
tryIt.solution: The rectangle's $2$ (through side-middles) plus its own $2$ diagonals: $2 + 2 = 4$.

tryIt.statement: Block letter H has $2$ lines of symmetry; block letter M has $1$. How many more has H?
tryIt.solution: $2 - 1 = 1$ more (the horizontal fold that M fails). Add back: $1 + 1 = 2$ ✓.

steps.title: The fold test
beats: Try the fold — this lesson's promise. Fold a shape along a line: if the halves lie exactly edge on edge, the line is a LINE OF SYMMETRY. Any overhang, however small, and it is not.
The dashed line in the picture is the triangle's one true mirror: it stands at the halfway mark of the base, $2 + 8 = 10$, $10 \div 2 = 5$, and rises through the apex.
Exact is the whole rule: two matching halves are each one half of the shape, and $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1$ — they rebuild it perfectly with nothing left over.

steps.title: Finding the fold
steps.intro: The mirror stands at the true middle — compute it, then fold.

examples.prompt: The triangle in the picture has base corners at $2$ and $8$, apex above the middle. Where is its mirror line, and how many does it have?
steps: Halfway between $2$ and $8$: $2 + 8 = 10$, $10 \div 2 = 5$ — the dashed vertical through the apex.
Fold there: the two slanted sides swap places exactly. No other fold matches: $1$ line.

examples.prompt: The rectangle in the picture runs from $1$ to $9$ across and $2$ to $6$ up. Find both mirror lines.
steps: Vertical: halfway between $1$ and $9$ — $1 + 9 = 10$, $10 \div 2 = 5$.
Horizontal: halfway between $2$ and $6$ — $2 + 6 = 8$, $8 \div 2 = 4$. Two lines, both dashed in the picture — and no diagonal fold matches.
examples.answer: the vertical at $5$ and the horizontal at $4$ — $2$ lines

steps.title: Fold and judge
steps.intro: Exact match or nothing.

problems.prompt: You fold a shape on a line and one half sticks out past the other. The line is:
options: a line of symmetry if the overhang is small
problems.explanation: The fold test is exact: a true mirror splits the shape into two matching halves, $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1$, with NOTHING left over. Overhang means the halves differ — test failed.

problems.prompt: The triangle in the picture has sides $8$, $6$ and $4$ — all different. Its lines of symmetry number:
problems.explanation: A fold must swap two EQUAL sides onto each other, but here no two sides match: $4 < 6$ and $6 < 8$. No fold works — a scalene triangle has no mirror.

problems.prompt: The triangle in the picture has base corners at $3$ and $9$ and two equal slanted sides. Its mirror line stands at:
problems.explanation: The true middle of the base: $3 + 9 = 12$, $12 \div 2 = 6$ — exactly where the dashed line is drawn. One line of symmetry.

steps.title: Exact or nothing
steps.prompt: The fold test passes only when:
options: the two halves match exactly, edge on edge
steps.explanation: Symmetry is an exact promise: each half is precisely one half, and $2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1$ — the two rebuild the whole with no overhang. Direction never matters: mirrors can stand upright, lie flat, or lean.

steps.title: You are built on a mirror line
steps.body: Most animals are: biologists call it BILATERAL symmetry. A butterfly's wing patterns match across its body line, left wing mirroring right — and your own face, hands and skeleton pair up across a line down your middle. Nature discovered the fold test long before geometry named it.

steps.title: Counting the lines
beats: Each shape carries a COUNT of working folds. The square in the picture has all four drawn: the vertical at $2 + 8 = 10$, $10 \div 2 = 5$, the horizontal at the same $5$ — and both diagonals, corner to corner.
That is the rectangle's $2$ plus the square's bonus $2$: $2 + 2 = 4$. Equal sides are what let the diagonal folds match.
Counts to remember: scalene triangle $0$, isosceles triangle $1$, rectangle $2$, square $4$. More rules kept, more mirrors earned.

steps.title: Symmetry numbers
steps.intro: Count the folds that pass; the count is the shape's property.

examples.prompt: Count the square's lines of symmetry.
steps: Side-middle folds: vertical and horizontal — $2$, the rectangle's pair.
Diagonal folds: both match, because all sides are equal — $2$ more. Total: $2 + 2 = 4$.

examples.prompt: How many MORE lines has a square than a (non-square) rectangle?
steps: Square $4$, rectangle $2$: the difference is $4 - 2 = 2$ — exactly the two diagonals.
Add back: $2 + 2 = 4$ ✓.

steps.title: Count the mirrors
steps.intro: Fold by fold — count only the folds that pass.

problems.prompt: Block letter H has how many lines of symmetry?
problems.explanation: A vertical fold matches its two uprights, and a horizontal fold matches top to bottom: $1 + 1 = 2$ lines.

problems.prompt: Which block letter has NO line of symmetry?
problems.explanation: A and T each pass one vertical fold ($1$ line each); F fails every fold — $0$. Their three counts: $0 + 1 + 1 = 2$ lines among them.

problems.prompt: The four-equal-sided shape in the picture (not a square) has its mirror lines along:
problems.explanation: Fold corner to corner and the equal sides swap exactly — both diagonals pass, standing at the true middles: across, $2 + 8 = 10$, $10 \div 2 = 5$; and up, $1 + 9 = 10$, $10 \div 2 = 5$. The side-middle folds fail because its corners are not right angles: $2$ lines, not $4$.

steps.title: Where the extra mirrors come from
steps.prompt: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry and a square has 4. The square's two extra lines run:
steps.explanation: Equal sides let the diagonal folds match: $4 - 2 = 2$ extra lines, and $2 + 2 = 4$ in all. The rectangle's unequal neighbours make its diagonal folds overhang.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The fold test: halves match exactly — line of symmetry; any overhang — not.
The mirror line passes the TRUE middle: halfway between 2 and 8 is exactly 5.
Counts: scalene 0, isosceles 1, rectangle 2, square 2 + 2 = 4.
A rectangle's diagonals are NOT mirror lines — only the square earns those.
Letters carry counts too: F 0, A 1, H 2.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each shape below, fold it in your head one line at a time and say pass or fail — then count the passes. The count is the answer.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Fold, judge, count.

problems.prompt: An isosceles triangle (two equal sides) has how many lines of symmetry?
problems.explanation: One fold — through the apex and the base's middle — swaps the two equal sides exactly. A scalene triangle, whose sides all differ, has no fold that works at all: $0 < 1$. So this one earns exactly $1$ line.

problems.prompt: A square, a rectangle and a scalene triangle: total lines of symmetry?
problems.explanation: $4 + 2 + 0 = 6$ lines among the three shapes.

problems.prompt: The rectangle in the picture shows its mirror lines dashed. How many are there — and are the diagonals included?
problems.explanation: Both side-middle folds pass, standing at the true middles: across, $2 + 8 = 10$ and $10 \div 2 = 5$; up, $1 + 9 = 10$ and $10 \div 2 = 5$ — exact, not roughly. Diagonal folds overhang: $2$ lines.

problems.prompt: The word MOM is written in block capitals. Total lines of symmetry, letter by letter?
problems.explanation: M has $1$ (vertical), O has $2$ (vertical and horizontal), M has $1$: $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$. That vertical mirror in every letter is why MOM reads the same in an actual mirror.

problems.prompt: A shape's mirror line must pass through:
options: the exact middle of what it splits
problems.explanation: Exact, always: for a base from $3$ to $9$ the mirror stands at $3 + 9 = 12$, $12 \div 2 = 6$ — one number, not a neighbourhood. (Some mirrors DO pass corners, like the square's diagonals, but only when the corner sits on the true middle line.)

steps.title: You've finished "Line Symmetry"
steps.body: The fold test, the true middle, and each shape's symmetry number. One promise left to test — and it needs all three dimensions: faces, edges and vertices of the solids in your hands.

lessons.title: 3-D Solids
lessons.concreteComparison: A dice, a brick, a ball, a tin can, an ice-cream cone and a point-topped tower: six solids you can hold. Flat shapes live on paper; solids fill your hand — so they need three counts, not one. FACES are the flat surfaces you can press a palm against, EDGES the lines where two faces meet, VERTICES the corner points. A dice: $6$ faces, $12$ edges, $8$ vertices — count one tonight.
lessons.objective: Name the six common solids — cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone, square pyramid — count faces, edges and vertices, and say which 2-D shape each flat face is.
concept: **Three counts describe a solid.** Faces (flat surfaces), edges (lines where two faces meet), vertices (corner points). The cube: $6$ faces in $3$ opposite pairs, $12$ edges ($4$ around the top, $4$ around the bottom, $4$ upright), $8$ vertices ($4$ up, $4$ down).

**Faces wear 2-D names.** A cube's faces are squares; a cuboid's are rectangles; a square pyramid wears $1$ square and $4$ triangles. The cylinder has $2$ circle faces and a curved wrap; the cone $1$ circle and a curved slope; the sphere is all curve — no flat face, no edge, no vertex.

**The counting receipt.** For solids with flat faces, faces plus vertices beats edges by exactly $2$: cube $6 + 8 - 12 = 2$, square pyramid $5 + 5 - 8 = 2$. Miscount anything and the receipt refuses to balance — it catches errors like a checksum.
lessons.keyIdea: Count three things — faces, edges, vertices — name each flat face with its 2-D shape, and receipt the count: faces plus vertices minus edges always makes 2.

facts.title: The cube's numbers
facts.explanation: Faces plus vertices minus edges makes 2 — the receipt that audits your counting.

facts.title: Faces wear 2-D names
facts.explanation: Every flat face of a solid is a 2-D shape you already know how to name.

workedExamples.statement: Count a dice: faces, edges, vertices — then run the receipt.
workedExamples.note: Count in groups: pairs of faces; top, bottom and upright edges.
workedExamples.solution: Faces: $3$ opposite pairs — $3 \times 2 = 6$. Edges: $4$ around the top, $4$ around the bottom, $4$ upright — $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$. Vertices: $4$ up, $4$ down — $4 + 4 = 8$. Receipt: $6 + 8 = 14$, and $14 - 12 = 2$ ✓ — the count balances.

workedExamples.statement: Count a square pyramid: faces, edges, vertices — and receipt it.
workedExamples.note: One base below, triangles rising to one apex.
workedExamples.solution: Faces: $1$ square base $+ 4$ triangles $= 5$. Vertices: $4$ base corners $+ 1$ apex $= 5$. Edges: $4$ around the base $+ 4$ rising to the apex $= 8$. Receipt: $5 + 5 = 10$, and $10 - 8 = 2$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Counting only the faces you can see in a drawing — calling a cube "3 faces".
commonMistakes.correction: A drawing hides the back, the bottom and one side. Count in opposite PAIRS — front-back, left-right, top-bottom: 3 × 2 = 6 — and the hidden ones stop escaping.
An edge is a LINE where two faces meet; a vertex is a POINT where edges meet. Run a finger along a dice: the finger slides along an edge and STOPS at a vertex.

tryIt.statement: A brick (a cuboid) — count its faces, edges and vertices, and run the receipt.
tryIt.solution: Same counts as the cube: $3 \times 2 = 6$ faces, $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ edges, $4 + 4 = 8$ vertices. Receipt: $6 + 8 - 12 = 2$ ✓ — only the face SHAPES differ (rectangles, not squares).

tryIt.statement: Which 2-D shapes are a cuboid's faces? And how many FLAT faces has a cylinder?
tryIt.solution: A cuboid wears $6$ rectangles (in $3$ equal pairs: $3 \times 2 = 6$). A cylinder has $1 + 1 = 2$ flat faces — both circles — plus one curved wrap that is not flat.

steps.title: Faces, edges, vertices
beats: Solids need THREE counts. FACES: the flat surfaces (a drawing hides some — the dashed lines in the picture mark hidden edges). EDGES: lines where two faces meet. VERTICES: points where edges meet.

Count the cube in groups, and the hidden parts cannot escape: faces in opposite pairs, $3 \times 2 = 6$; edges as top ring, bottom ring, uprights, $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$; vertices as $4$ up and $4$ down, $4 + 4 = 8$.
Then RECEIPT the count: faces plus vertices minus edges must make $2$. Cube: $6 + 8 = 14$, $14 - 12 = 2$ ✓. If your receipt says anything else, a count is wrong.

steps.title: Counting solids
steps.intro: Groups first, then the receipt.

examples.prompt: A dice: count faces, edges and vertices, and receipt the count.
steps: Faces $3 \times 2 = 6$; edges $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$; vertices $4 + 4 = 8$.

examples.prompt: A cuboid brick — same counts as the cube?
steps: Yes: $6$ faces, $12$ edges, $8$ vertices — the receipt balances the same way, $6 + 8 - 12 = 2$.
The difference is the face SHAPES: rectangles instead of squares.

steps.title: Count the dice
steps.intro: Pairs, rings, and the receipt.

problems.prompt: A cube has how many faces?
problems.explanation: Three opposite pairs: $3 \times 2 = 6$. (Answering $4$ counts only what a drawing shows; $8$ counts the vertices.)

problems.prompt: A cube has how many edges?
problems.explanation: Top ring $4$, bottom ring $4$, uprights $4$: $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$.

problems.prompt: For a cuboid, faces plus vertices minus edges makes:
problems.explanation: $6 + 8 = 14$, and $14 - 12 = 2$ (add back: $2 + 12 = 14$ ✓). The $26$ is what you get ADDING all three counts instead.

steps.title: The hidden faces
steps.prompt: In a drawing of a dice you can see 3 faces. How many are hidden?
steps.explanation: The dice has $6$ in all: $6 - 3 = 3$ hidden (back, bottom and one side). Add back: $3 + 3 = 6$ ✓ — count in pairs and the hidden ones stop escaping.

steps.title: The dice's secret sevens
steps.body: On a standard dice, opposite faces always add to $7$: $1 + 6$, $2 + 5$, $3 + 4$. Three pairs of opposite faces, three sums, one answer. Pick up any board-game dice and check — and notice the pairing uses each number from $1$ to $6$ exactly once.

steps.title: Round solids and the pyramid
beats: Not every solid is a box. The SPHERE (ball) is all curve: $0$ flat faces, $0$ edges, $0$ vertices. The CYLINDER (tin can): $2$ circle faces and a curved wrap. The CONE (ice-cream cone): $1$ circle face and a curved slope to a point.
The SQUARE PYRAMID in the picture is flat-faced through and through: $1$ square base $+ 4$ triangles $= 5$ faces, $4 + 1 = 5$ vertices, $4 + 4 = 8$ edges.
Its receipt balances too: $5 + 5 = 10$, $10 - 8 = 2$ ✓. Every flat-faced solid signs the same receipt — the round ones play by their own curved rules.

steps.title: Pyramids and round solids
steps.intro: Name the faces, then receipt the flat-faced solids.

examples.prompt: The square pyramid: which 2-D shapes are its faces, and does the receipt balance?
steps: $1$ square (the base) $+ 4$ triangles (the slopes) $= 5$ faces.

examples.prompt: Flat faces of the round solids: cylinder, cone, sphere — total?
steps: Cylinder $2$ circles, cone $1$ circle, sphere none.
Total: $2 + 1 + 0 = 3$ flat faces among the three of them.

steps.title: Round and pointed
steps.intro: Faces wear 2-D names.

problems.prompt: A square pyramid's faces are:
problems.explanation: One square base below, four triangle slopes meeting at the apex: $1 + 4 = 5$ faces.

problems.prompt: Which solid has NO flat face, NO edge and NO vertex?
problems.explanation: The ball is all curve. The cylinder keeps $1 + 1 = 2$ flat circle faces; the cube is flat everywhere.

problems.prompt: A square pyramid has how many vertices?
problems.explanation: $4$ base corners $+ 1$ apex $= 5$. ($4$ forgets the apex; $8$ counts the edges.) Receipt: $5 + 5 - 8 = 2$ ✓.

steps.title: The receipt catches it
steps.prompt: A student counts a cuboid: 6 faces, 8 vertices, 11 edges. What does the receipt say?
steps.explanation: $6 + 8 = 14$, and $14 - 11 = 3$ (add back: $3 + 11 = 14$). A balanced count makes exactly $2$, so something was miscounted — it is the edges: a cuboid has $12$, and $6 + 8 - 12 = 2$ ✓.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Three counts describe a solid: faces (flat surfaces), edges (meeting lines), vertices (corner points).
Cube and cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices — count in pairs and rings.
Faces wear 2-D names: squares, rectangles, the pyramid's 1 square + 4 triangles.
Sphere: no face, edge or vertex; cylinder: 2 circle faces; cone: 1.
The receipt: faces + vertices − edges = 2 for every flat-faced solid — it audits your count.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every solid below, count in groups — pairs of faces, rings of edges — then run the receipt before you answer. If it makes anything but 2, recount.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: All six solids, all three counts.

problems.prompt: Faces, edges and vertices of a cube, all added together:
problems.explanation: $6 + 12 + 8 = 26$. (The receipt is different arithmetic: $6 + 8 - 12 = 2$.)

problems.prompt: Which solid rolls AND has two flat circle faces?
problems.explanation: The tin can: $1 + 1 = 2$ circle faces and a curved wrap between them. The cone has just $1$ circle; the sphere none.

problems.prompt: The square pyramid in the picture has how many edges?
problems.explanation: $4$ around the base $+ 4$ rising to the apex $= 8$. Receipt: $5 + 5 - 8 = 2$ ✓.

problems.prompt: A cuboid brick's faces are which 2-D shape?
problems.explanation: Six rectangles, in $3$ equal opposite pairs: $3 \times 2 = 6$. (A cube is the special cuboid whose rectangles are all squares.)

problems.prompt: The cube's receipt and the pyramid's receipt both make:
problems.explanation: Cube: $6 + 8 - 12 = 2$. Pyramid: $5 + 5 - 8 = 2$. Same answer from different counts — that is what makes the receipt worth running.

steps.title: You've finished "3-D Solids" — and the topic
steps.body: Count the sides, test the corners, try the fold — and now count the faces, edges and vertices too. Every promise a shape makes came with a test, and every test came with a receipt. Grade 5 geometry picks up from here: measuring the boundary and counting the inside.

practice.statement: The shape in the picture has $5$ straight sides. Name it, and count its vertices with the side-ends receipt.
practice.solution: Five sides: a PENTAGON. Ends: $5 \times 2 = 10$; each vertex joins $2$ ends: $10 \div 2 = 5$ vertices — corners match sides.

practice.statement: How many right angles fill a straight line? A full turn? Show both with the quarter-turn arithmetic.
practice.solution: A straight line is half a turn: $2 \times 90 = 180$, so $2$ right angles. A full turn: $4 \times 90 = 360$, so $360 \div 90 = 4$.

practice.statement: The rectangle in the picture has corners $(1, 1)$, $(8, 1)$, $(8, 5)$, $(1, 5)$. Check its opposite sides are equal, and say why it is not a square.
practice.solution: Bottom and top: $8 - 1 = 7$ each (add back $7 + 1 = 8$ ✓). Left and right: $5 - 1 = 4$ each ($4 + 1 = 5$ ✓). Opposite pairs match: a rectangle. But $7 > 4$ — neighbouring sides differ, so it is not a square.

practice.statement: A student says a square is not a rectangle. Run the rectangle's two tests on a square and settle it.
practice.solution: Test 1 — four right angles: yes, $4 \times 90 = 360$, a full turn of page corners. Test 2 — opposite sides equal: yes, ALL its sides are equal. Both passed: $1 + 1 = 2$. Every square IS a rectangle; the equal sides are a bonus, not a fault.

practice.statement: The square in the picture shows its mirror lines dashed. How many are there, and where does the vertical one stand?
practice.solution: Four: the rectangle's $2$ side-middle lines plus the square's $2$ diagonals — $2 + 2 = 4$. The vertical stands at the true middle: $2 + 8 = 10$, $10 \div 2 = 5$.

practice.statement: Count the lines of symmetry of the block letters M, O, M — and the total for the word MOM.
practice.solution: M: $1$ vertical line. O: $2$ — vertical and horizontal. M: $1$. Total: $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$ — and the shared vertical mirror is why MOM survives a real mirror unchanged.

practice.statement: Count the cube in the picture — faces, edges, vertices — and run the receipt.
practice.solution: Faces in opposite pairs: $3 \times 2 = 6$. Edges as rings and uprights: $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$. Vertices: $4 + 4 = 8$. Receipt: $6 + 8 = 14$, $14 - 12 = 2$ ✓ (add back: $2 + 12 = 14$).

practice.statement: A square pyramid: name its faces with their 2-D shapes, count everything, and receipt the count.
practice.solution: Faces: $1$ square base $+ 4$ triangles $= 5$. Vertices: $4$ base corners $+ 1$ apex $= 5$. Edges: $4 + 4 = 8$. Receipt: $5 + 5 = 10$, $10 - 8 = 2$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: Name the shape in the picture, and use the side-ends receipt to count its vertices.
testYourself.solution: Six straight sides: a HEXAGON. Ends: $6 \times 2 = 12$; vertices: $12 \div 2 = 6$ — the corners match the sides.

testYourself.statement: A dancer makes three quarter turns, always the same way. How much of a full turn is that — and how much more would close the spin?
testYourself.solution: Three quarters: $3 \times 90 = 270$ degrees. The full turn is $360$, so one more quarter closes it: $360 - 270 = 90$, and $270 + 90 = 360$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: The shape in the picture has corners $(1, 2)$, $(9, 2)$, $(9, 6)$, $(1, 6)$, all right angles. Sort it: quadrilateral, rectangle, or square?
testYourself.solution: Opposite sides: $9 - 1 = 8$ and $8$ ($8 + 1 = 9$ ✓); $6 - 2 = 4$ and $4$ ($4 + 2 = 6$ ✓). Right angles and matching opposite pairs: a RECTANGLE. Not a square: $8 > 4$. (It is also a quadrilateral — the family holds all its members.)

testYourself.statement: A rectangle has $2$ lines of symmetry and a square has $4$. How many more has the square, and where do the extra ones run?
testYourself.solution: $4 - 2 = 2$ more (add back: $2 + 2 = 4$ ✓) — the two diagonals, corner to corner. The rectangle's diagonal folds overhang, because its neighbouring sides differ.

testYourself.statement: Count a cuboid's faces, edges and vertices, and prove the count balanced with the receipt.
testYourself.solution: Faces: $3 \times 2 = 6$; edges: $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$; vertices: $4 + 4 = 8$. Receipt: $6 + 8 = 14$, $14 - 12 = 2$ ✓ — a balanced count.

testYourself.statement: The square pyramid in the picture wears $1$ square face and $4$ triangle faces. Count the faces — and then count the SIDES of all five faces put together.
testYourself.solution: Faces: $1 + 4 = 5$. Sides of the faces: the square brings $4$, each triangle brings $3$ — $4 + 4 \times 3 = 4 + 12 = 16$ sides drawn across the five faces. (Fewer edges than that — $8$ — because on the solid, faces share their edges in pairs: $16 \div 2 = 8$.)
